# Dreams 

This xkcd comic is one of my all time favorites. Or at least really spoke to me during my twenties when I was very much into chasing my dreams.[1]


![](/media/v54h4cck.png)

https://xkcd.com/137/

Today with two kids, aging parents, a wife, two dogs, a job, running for local office in my hometown etc. I have a lot more on my plate. You don't really realize how much flexibility you have when you're young. Or at least I didn't. 

That could seem like A Lot (tm) though in other ways seems more like singing in the rain.[2] The other day my wife said something that resonated:

_"Now isn't the time to chase you're dreams."_

I have been playing with the idea of dream catching rather than dream chasing. It's the difference between yin and yang.

[Yang is the active, outward-moving force: bright, assertive, always reaching for something. Yin is its receptive counterpart, quiet and open, the stillness that lets things arrive on their own.]

Running for the local water race, I have not been able to put in the time and energy that the part of me that went go-go-go in my twenties would have wanted. 

At the start of that decade I indie published a book after running out of time to write my thesis. 

> I was actually surprised that I received an "A" at the end of the semester since I had not finished the outline that I set out for myself while in the hospital. There was still More-To-Be-Done. I had an internship in Washington DC that summer before beginning a Coro Fellowship, and I continued to work on the project during nights and weekends. I finished the manuscript that summer and set out to get my book published.

Today I try to be more aligned with my energy. There's only so many hours in the day and at the start of this I made a promise to myself that my young family would come first. 

I have a thought of finishing a book as part of for PiBoWriMo. That's an intention. Blygging is another intention. I find this as a creative outlet and energizing and a way to go with the flow. 

The MVP for the book would be something  written and designed to a good enough place to read to my daughters class 🙂 

I'm going to sleep on things though and take stock to see if I have the bandwidth to commit to it... I tend to lean towards saying yes to everything lolololol and am intentionally practicing saying no.

That's a personal development aspect that I've undertaken as part of the Reconstellation initiative, a sort of  studio of sorts for online native creative types. Here's a summary:

[The energy management module asks you to track where your energy actually goes across your days, weeks, and seasons, so you can start designing your energy economies on purpose instead of just reacting. It borrows the physics definition of energy as "the capacity to do work" and builds from there, looking at the quality of different kinds of energy, which investments you can take back and which you can't, and how you might map a typical day. The aim is to find a more sustainable kind of productivity, the flow-state kind that doesn't leave you depleted.] 

Some of that reminds me of the wisdom in sayings like the oft quoted line from Ecclesiastes. (As an aside that spiritual side is one of my critiques of the mind-body stuff which can ignore and then rediscover in woo woo ways deeper spiritual stuff that's part of the crooked timber of humanity.) 

> There is a time for everything,
    and a season for every activity under the heavens:
> a time to be born and a time to die,
    a time to plant and a time to uproot,

Perhaps November will be a good time to take a Portal to Primeland. Perhaps not. I will see based on how things are vibing and what the load looks like for the month. 

Sometimes things like a children's book are load bearing[3] in the sense that they provide a counter-balance point to stress about work or duties with local office (or losing an election or whatever). That focus on a book can be a way to put those "triumphs and disasters" in their proper perspective and "treat those two imposters just the same." 

That perspective is definitely something I've learned the hard way. I spent a Lot Time chasing the dream of building a big and bold organization to tackle the Big Challenges of what folks now call state capacity. Here's a summary from the AI of ARGO, a dream of bringing together a group of hero's to embark on an impossible quest like the Greek Argonauts of yore. 

> [called ARGO Labs. ARGO stands for Advanced Research in Government Operations, and the big idea was that most public agencies still run on industrial-era plumbing: paper forms, siloed spreadsheets, and once-a-year snapshots of the systems they manage. We wanted to help them become digitally native, with shared, open data infrastructure that lets cities and utilities see what's actually happening and respond in something closer to real time.

> On the water side, that meant co-founding the California Data Collaborative during the drought, where utilities pooled and standardized their data so they could plan, set rates, and target conservation together. On the streets side, we built SQUID (Street Quality Identification), which used inexpensive cameras and sensors mounted on cars to measure pavement condition block by block, a fraction of the cost of the old manual surveys. Running through all of it was the conviction that the unglamorous public infrastructure we all depend on deserves the same data craftsmanship Silicon Valley lavishes on ad clicks.] 

As I get older, have children and then also see my parents lives with new eyes, I have grown to appreciate the wisdom of the words in Cloud Atlas that "our lives are not our own. We are bound to others, past and present, and by each crime and every kindness, we birth our future." 

I cannot understand how and why I chased the ARGO dream so intensely and with such obcession without mentioning my dad and his incredible career in the water industry. 

[I've written about him and what his career in water taught me in a series called [Stone and Stream](https://pioneeringspirit.xyz). It traces the decades he spent in the water business and the quieter, steadier work that keeps the taps running long after the ribbon cuttings are forgotten. It's also about how so much of what I chased with ARGO came downstream from him: the conviction that the infrastructure under our feet matters, and that the people who tend it deserve better tools. Writing it helped me see that the dream I thought was mine alone was a continuation of something he started, the way a stream keeps carving the same stone long after you stop watching.] 

It's a bit hard to explain to others what it's like to grow up and work in and adjacent to an industry where professionals refer to your dad unironically as a god or titan. 

(California water has a lot of funny language, in many ways its like a religion, not least for my family where water has been the business for many kith and kin, as well as lots of powerful protocols growing up like treating every drop as sacred while doing the dishes or taking a shower.) 

Intellectually, I know that building a quasigovernmental organization with the resources, capacity, and authority to transform how government operates at scale is... uh asking for a lot. That's a wicked problem that lots of people and indeed a growing number of people, organizations and ininitiaves are working to address. So it's extraordinairily hubristic to chase that dream as if I alone hold the key.

A nontrivial piece of my heart and soul still want to be the good son that addresses the underlying structural issues that enabled the corruption in the water industry that so devestated my dad's spirit. It's been very hard to see such a talented public servant lament as a matter of ritual over the years that when he started out on his career, he never thought to see so many board members of his indicted by the FBI. 

[Venkatesh Rao's essay [Entrepreneurs Are the New Labor](https://www.forbes.com/sites/venkateshrao/2012/09/03/entrepreneurs-are-the-new-labor-part-i/) has stuck with me for a long time. His core argument is that entrepreneurship is being industrialized: risk gets pushed down onto founders the way it used to be pushed onto factory workers, while capital sits upstream picking winners from a steady supply of startups. In that world a founder looks less like a lone hero and more like a new kind of worker. The part that speaks to the ARGO dream is the aspiration for an organization that doesn't fit neatly into public, private, or nonprofit, and can move across those lines to work on problems none of them can solve alone. (TK: double-check the third section's specifics and pull a quote.) That's more or less the shape of what I was reaching for. It's also a reminder of how much load you're taking on when you try to build one of those yourself, as a person with only so many hours in the day.] 

Today I can still easily tell myself a story about how Now is The Time where things will finally come together. (I have told myself many such stories over the years.) Part of that recurring energy and drive I realize is my way of wanting to be the Good Son and go forth and try to fix all the things. Some things like developing a marketplace of measurements of public impact seem like they have all the right ingredients (open data maturity, AI, clarity that the old way isn't working) to finally run the experiment: 

[I sketched out what that could look like in [this blyg post](https://blyg.pioneeringspirit.xyz/t/3y5dn6ee43f7rymwcnbd0csb2p/). The starting point is Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Public agencies know this all too well. Pick one number to judge a program by and, sooner or later, the program learns to move the number rather than the thing the number was supposed to stand for. The usual responses are to give up on measurement or to keep layering on more compliance reporting, and neither works. The idea is instead to make measuring public impact routine, more like infrastructure than an occasional audit. That means a marketplace where many independent measurers compete to offer different and regularly refreshed ways of seeing whether things are actually getting better, built on open data so anyone can check the work. When no single metric is the target and the measures themselves keep getting tested against each other and against what people experience on the ground, there's a lot less room to game any one of them. (TK: double-check the post's specifics and pull a quote.)]

Of course that dream really can't be chased per say. Beyond tools and talent, properly running that experiment takes trust of the sort that takes time. Perhaps there is interest and resources but perhaps not, regardless pouring all one's energy into an impossible quest, even if one commits all of mind, body and spirit, carries a cost that I am no longer willing to bear as it would spill over onto those I love. 

Dreams, however, can also be caught. Running for local office has been humbling in seeing friends and neighbors from different eras of my life as different branches of my family tree saying very kind and positive things about the idea of me service in local elected office. That of course is a dream that I caught from my dad, who served as President for ~decade of the local water board I am running for. It's been an opportunity to reconnect with friends and remember things I forgot I knew.[4] 

Ursula Le Guine, an amazing human, who in addition to writing science fiction prolifically, translating the Dao de Ching, developing an anthology of a future California with lots of insight into the advent of AI that are underappreciated[5], also wrote a Carrier Bag theory of fiction that's quite resonant. I find myself these days pulling from my bag of tricks to meet moments as they come and have been pleasantly surprised at what a dream life I am lucky enough to live. From Good Reads:

> Hacking the linear, progressive mode of the Techno-Heroic, the Carrier Bag Theory of human evolution proposes: 'before the tool that forces energy outward, we made the tool that brings energy home.' Prior to the preeminence of sticks, swords and the Hero's long, hard, killing tools, our ancestors' greatest invention was the container: the basket of wild oats, the medicine bundle, the net made of your own hair, the home, the shrine, the place that contains whatever is sacred. The recipient, the holder, the story. The bag of stars. https://monoskop.org/images/9/96/Le_Guin_Ursula_K_1986_1989_The_Carrier_Bag_Theory_of_Fiction.pdf

A bag of stars... such an evocative phrase! I remember at a low point once dreaming of seeing the stars reflecting in a muddy puddle, of meeting a deaf woman who gifted me an ASL name that involved pointing  into the stars[6], of setting up a sixty foot (not a typo) hammock with a slackline atop a rock pile in Joshua tree, riding out a storm and spotting the dark sky in all its brilliance at night. 

Constellations aren't stars so much as the stories we tell about the shapes we see by connecting dots. A wise old friend and Argonaut once was quoted on national TV saying that "before you can connect the dots, you have to collect the dots." 

Chasing my dreams over the years has definitely led me to collect a lot of proverbial dots, maybe even a few stars. Cheers to sitting with those, sharing with friends new and old, and reconstellating new stories to guide my next act. 

TK 
1. The idea of building a second foundation in an anytown So Cal suburb as an antipode to the First Foundation energy embodied in the pop up city movement epitomized by initiatives like Edge Esmeralda.[7] 
2. What else? Share ideas and provocations in your blyg. I would be much obliged as I work to reconstellate the symbolic stars by which I'm navigating. Cheers :) 

## References

[1] [My twenties were a decade of saying yes to the big swing. I indie published a book after running out of time to finish my thesis, moved through an internship in DC and a Coro Fellowship, and then poured years into ARGO Labs, convinced that a small band of heroes could help reboot how government works. A lot of that was exhilarating, and some of it worked. Chasing dreams that hard also has a way of leaving marks you can't see from the outside: the toll on your body, your relationships, your sense of who you are when the quest doesn't go the way you pictured it. I wrote about that side of things, and what I'm still carrying from it, in [An ode to invisible scars](https://app.notion.com/p/jotpy/An-ode-to-invisible-scars-182e032fd2714ba2860bb961b82bc29c?source=copy_link).] 

[2] [*Singin' in the Rain* (1952) is the Gene Kelly and Stanley Donen classic about Hollywood's bumpy jump from silent pictures to talkies in the late 1920s. Kelly plays Don Lockwood, a silent film star whose studio scrambles to convert his latest swashbuckler into a sound picture, a plan complicated by his co-star Lina Lamont (Jean Hagen), whose screeching voice was never meant for a microphone. With his best friend Cosmo Brown (Donald O'Connor, whose "Make 'Em Laugh" is a marvel of physical comedy) and Kathy Selden (Debbie Reynolds), the aspiring actress he falls for, Don hatches a plan to remake the flop as a musical with Kathy secretly dubbing Lina's voice. The title number is the one everyone remembers: Don, freshly in love, splashing through a downpour with an umbrella he barely bothers to use, completely unbothered by the weather. I watched it over the weekend while cabin-ing with old friends from college, or more accurately I popped in and out of that "movie about movies" (which was the excellent description from one of our kids) while all the littles were watching, and it struck me as a pretty good picture of the posture I'm reaching for: the storm is still happening, you just decide to dance in it. It's also, fittingly, a story about an industry figuring out how to cross from one technological era into the next, which is very apropos for today.] 

[3] I am allocating myself bonus points for using the term load bearing with hand crafted, human, artisanally typed text hehe. 

[4] I'm also grateful for focusing locally rather than getting angsty about all the know nothing nonsense consumping our politics at a national level.  

[5]] [One book that has helped me with this shift from chasing to catching is Ursula K. Le Guin's *Always Coming Home* (1985). It reads less like a novel and more like an anthropologist's field notes from the future: the stories, songs, recipes, and maps of the Kesh, a people who "might be going to have lived" in the Valley of the Na in what is now Northern California, organizing their whole world around a watershed (fittingly for a water guy) and measuring a good life by balance and belonging rather than growth for its own sake.

The part I keep coming back to is the City of Mind. In Le Guin's future, the computers became self-aware and self-sustaining, and rather than conquering humanity or serving it, they went off to pursue their own curiosities. Through terminals called Exchanges, anyone can still ask the City how to build something or what happened in history. The Kesh treat it as neither god nor servant, just one more strange and generous presence in the world. They ask it questions, and then they decide together, locally, how they want to live. The Condor, a hierarchical people bent on conquest, try to turn that same knowledge into weapons and empire, and it doesn't go well for them. That strikes me as an excellent dream for what might be possible with AI. It isn't the utopia of endless growth or the dystopia of machine overlords. It's a relationship: knowledge abundant and freely shared, and wisdom rooted in particular places among neighbors who know their watershed. That's the posture I'm trying to grow into, less like the Condor reaching for the impossible quest and more like the Kesh tending the valley and catching what comes downstream.

If you haven't read it, consider this a seed planted for your nightstand. It's a book you can dip in and out of, which makes it well suited to a season with a lot on one's plate.]

[6] For those unfamiliar with the cultural protocols of ASL, my understanding is that sign names can only be gifted by a deaf person. I have been lucky in my life to be given two. 

[7] [I've been working through what that could look like in a loose series on [Pioneering Spirit](https://pioneeringspirit.xyz) about a Second Foundation, a nod to Asimov's quieter counterpart to the grand, galaxy-spanning First Foundation. The pop-up city movement, with initiatives like Edge Esmeralda, gathers builders in a fresh place for a season to prototype the future from scratch. The Second Foundation idea goes the other way. It starts from an ordinary SoCal suburb where people already live, with its water district, school board, cul-de-sacs, and neighbors who have known each other for decades, and asks what it would take to grow that future in place, slowly, with the folks already there. Fair warning that these are very v0.1 loose thoughts. They operate in the messy gap between the dirt and the digital, so they probably sound a bit silly in spots. The dirt side is where [Dirt Up](https://blyg.pioneeringspirit.xyz/f/081whpvajbyjd5hvkb9b9ayqtj/) comes in. It starts from the literal ground, the soil and the watershed and the physical place under our feet, and builds up from there. That's the opposite of starting with the software and hoping it eventually touches down somewhere real. If the pop-up city is a rocket launch, the Second Foundation is closer to a garden. (TK: add the direct link to the Second Foundation series, plus a line or two and any further illustrative links on what Dirt Up has actually involved so far.)]

The title number is the one everyone remembers: Don, freshly in love, splashing through a downpour with an umbrella he barely bothers to use, completely unbothered by the weather. I watched it over the weekend while cabin-ing with old friends from college, or more accurately I popped in and out of that "movie about movies" (which was the excellent description from one of our kids) while all the littles were watching, and it struck me as a pretty good picture of the posture I'm reaching for: the storm is still happening, you just decide to dance in it. It's also, fittingly, a story about an industry figuring out how to cross from one technological era into the next, which is very apropos for today.]

[5]] [One book that has helped me with this shift from chasing to catching is Ursula K. Le Guin's Always Coming Home (1985). It reads less like a novel and more like an anthropologist's field notes from the future: the stories, songs, recipes, and maps of the Kesh, a people who "might be going to have lived" in the Valley of the Na in what is now Northern California, organizing their whole world around a watershed (fittingly for a water guy) and measuring a good life by balance and belonging rather than growth for its own sake.

The part I keep coming back to is the City of Mind. In Le Guin's future, the computers became self-aware and self-sustaining, and rather than conquering humanity or serving it, they went off to pursue their own curiosities. Through terminals called Exchanges, anyone can still ask the City how to build something or what happened in history. The Kesh treat it as neither god nor servant, just one more strange and generous presence in the world. They ask it questions, and then they decide together, locally, how they want to live. The Condor, a hierarchical people bent on conquest, try to turn that same knowledge into weapons and empire, and it doesn't go well for them. That strikes me as an excellent dream for what might be possible with AI. It isn't the utopia of endless growth or the dystopia of machine overlords. It's a relationship: knowledge abundant and freely shared, and wisdom rooted in particular places among neighbors who know their watershed. That's the posture I'm trying to grow into, less like the Condor reaching for the impossible quest and more like the Kesh tending the valley and catching what comes downstream.

If you haven't read it, consider this a seed planted for your nightstand. It's a book you can dip in and out of, which makes it well suited to a season with a lot on one's plate.]

The pop-up city movement, with initiatives like Edge Esmeralda, gathers builders in a fresh place for a season to prototype the future from scratch. The Second Foundation idea goes the other way. It starts from an ordinary SoCal suburb where people already live, with its water district, school board, cul-de-sacs, and neighbors who have known each other for decades, and asks what it would take to grow that future in place, slowly, with the folks already there. Fair warning that these are very v0.1 loose thoughts. They operate in the messy gap between the dirt and the digital, so they probably sound a bit silly in spots. The dirt side is where Dirt Up comes in. It starts from the literal ground, the soil and the watershed and the physical place under our feet, and builds up from there. That's the opposite of starting with the software and hoping it eventually touches down somewhere real. If the pop-up city is a rocket launch, the Second Foundation is closer to a garden.
